source.title: The Vanishing Decision Boundary Complexity and the Strong First Component

record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses double descent in its background, but its own experiments do not test the claim versions: they do not measure test error across model size, epochs, or training-sample size, or locate interpolation peaks.
record.gate_note: The paper cites prior work on double descent and describes its own findings on decision-boundary evolution and optimizer-associated spectral properties. The optimizer/test-accuracy results below relate generalization to spectral properties, but do not test whether any double-descent curve or peak occurs.
record.test_reason: Double descent appears only in background (Section 2.3 summarizes Belkin et al. and Somepalli et al.). The paper's own experiments are decision-boundary visualizations and optimizer/architecture spectral profiling of VGG19, ResNet18 and DLA on CIFAR-10. None sweeps model size, epochs, sample count, label noise or regularization to trace a test-error curve or locate an interpolation peak. Its finding that annealed optimizers reaching ~100% train accuracy generalize better than ones at 99.3-99.7% compares optimizers. It is not an epoch-wise or model-wise test-error curve.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that complex decision-boundary structure is transient and vanishes in well-trained deep models, and that predecessor-model boundaries on training data indicate final generalization. They also find that the first principal component grows dominant and alone fits the training data. Optimizers show a 'singularity' link between auto-correlation rank reduction and better generalization. Skip connections balance first-component dominance and use all feature dimensions. They also argue that overfitting in deep learning has a different, beneficial effect compared with classical machine learning.
record.recipe_differences: The paper does not reproduce or implement the original double-descent method; it studies decision-boundary evolution and optimizer properties.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported generalization and spectral comparisons vary with optimizer and architecture; the paper also compares optimizer settings with and without learning-rate annealing.

fits_no_version.finding: For VGG19 on CIFAR-10, optimizers with a slightly reduced-rank auto-correlation matrix (Adadelta 91.9%, Adam 92.6%) beat full-rank ones (ASGD and Adagrad, 90.6%). RAdam (93%) is a full-rank exception.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Rank and leading singular values of the last-layer feature auto-correlation matrix correlate with optimizer generalization.

fits_no_version.finding: Non-SGD optimizers trained with learning-rate annealing to near 100% train accuracy (Fig. 4) generalize better than the same optimizers without annealing (Fig. 5, 99.3-99.7% train accuracy). Values are given in figures only.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Training closer to full interpolation improves test accuracy across optimizers. This compares optimizer settings and is not a double-descent curve.

record.problems: The paper does not test the claim's size, epoch, or sample-size curves. The optimizer generalization profiles are presented as figures, and the text gives only some optimizer accuracy values; no uncertainty estimates are stated.
record.rows_left_out: No additional double-descent results are reported. The decision-boundary visualizations and other optimizer/architecture comparisons do not measure a claim version.

untested.parts: All: no model-size sweep or interpolation-threshold peak.
All: no test error tracked over epochs for a fall-rise-fall shape.
All: no variation of training-sample count.
All: no capacity sweep across model classes.
All: no effective-complexity measure predicting peak location.
All: no label-noise, multiple-peak or tuned-regularization experiments.
All: no recounting of effective parameters against a risk curve.

record.verdict_notes: Single-author preprint. No uncertainty estimates are reported, and most numbers appear only in figures. Double descent is cited only in background (Belkin et al. [3], Somepalli et al. [62]); no claim version is tested.

versions.untested_parts: Model-size sweep, interpolation threshold, and fall-rise-fall test-error shape.
Test error over training epochs and the claimed fall-rise-fall shape.
Varying training-sample size near an interpolation threshold.
Double-descent risk curves across model classes and capacity.
Whether one effective-complexity measure predicts peak locations across size, epochs, or sample count.
Effects of label noise, multiple peaks, and optimally tuned regularization on a double-descent peak.
Whether re-counting complexity as effective parameters converts second descent into an ordinary U-shaped curve.
